newsitem.title: USA: Swiss envoy seeks Jewish nod on Holocaust gold.
newsitem.headline: Swiss envoy seeks Jewish nod on Holocaust gold.

text.p: Switzerland's ambassador to the United States warned a Jewish group on Tuesday not to underappreciate his country's belated drive to make amends for its handling of gold looted by Nazi Germany.

In a comment that drew an angry reply from a Jewish leader, Ambassador Alfred Defago told the national leadership conference of the Anti-Defamation League: "My people increasingly have the impression that, despite all the efforts of the past few months, the Swiss efforts are not appreciated or are only very underappreciated in the U.S.A."

Citing what he called "undifferentiated Switzerland bashing" by some U.S. politicians and media outlets, Defago warned that this was leading to "an increasing feeling of frustration, anger and bitterness."
"This is not a good development," he added. "In a country where the people have the last say through referendums, this is particularly problematic."
Defago's reference to underappreciation drew a blistering response from Abraham Foxman, national director of the Anti-Defamation League.
"In truth, you were dragged there. In truth, you were forced there," Foxman thundered from the podium, referring to the compensatory steps Switzerland has taken recently.
"...had others not yelled and screamed and embarassed, and had the United States not taken that courageous step, it probably would not have happened," Foxman said.

Meanwhile, the World Jewish Congress in New York asked on Tuesday that new aid for Holocaust survivors included in a proposed $5 billion Swiss fund for world disaster victims be placed instead into an already established fund for Hitler's Second World War victims.

WJC Vice President Kalman Sultanik said the proposal was aimed at taking the issue of Nazi gold reparations out of the internal Swiss debate over the proposed "Solidarity Fund," which some analysts doubt will be approved by Swiss voters.

Sultanik said that instead, the portion of the new money earmarked for Holocaust survivors should be placed in Switzerland's existing Holocaust Fund, which has so far received pledges of about $190 million from Swiss banks and businesses but nothing from the Swiss government.
He added that this would both keep the two issues separate and make the Holocaust monies available before the estimated eight years it would take to set up the Solidarity Fund.
"By then most Holocaust survivors will be dead," Sultanik said.
Last week, President Bill Clinton praised the Swiss government's "courageous proposals" for dealing with the looted gold issue and commended its willingness to help bring historical facts to light.

Clinton spoke after a U.S. undersecretary of commerce, Stuart Eizenstat, faulted Switzerland in a major report for an "obdurate reluctance" after the Second World War to cooperate with Allied efforts to find and redistribute ill-gotten gains.

Defago told the Anti-Defamation League, which calls itself the world's largest group fighting anti-Semitism, that Switzerland "has been experiencing the delayed trauma of recognising its imperfections as a nation."

He listed Swiss remediary measures, including the creation this month of a "Committee of Eminent Persons," headed by Paul Volcker, former chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve, to seach for dormant Jewish assets that may still be in Swiss banks.
Eizenstat, who also addressed the League on Tuesday, applauded the Swiss decision to document Switzerland's entire relationship with the Nazis, but urged this be done "promptly."
He described Swiss actions so far as important first steps. "And we hope that Switzerland will complete the journey by taking more," Eizenstat said.
